drills.q: Define Recall@k and Precision@k precisely. When should a RAG system optimize primarily for one over the other?
drills.a: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top-k|/|relevant|; Precision@k = |relevant ∩ top-k|/k. A RAG system whose generator reads the whole top-k context should optimize primarily for Recall@k -- getting the answer into context matters more than position -- with Precision@k as a secondary noise/cost concern.

drills.q: What's the difference between MRR and MAP, and when would you pick one over the other?
drills.a: MRR averages the reciprocal rank of only the first relevant result, blind to further relevant documents. MAP averages precision at every rank a relevant document appears, crediting multiple hits found early. Pick MRR for single-best-answer lookups (FAQ); pick MAP when multiple relevant documents add product value (multi-source synthesis).

drills.q: Derive nDCG and explain why you normalize by IDCG instead of using raw DCG.
drills.a: DCG@k = sum(rel_i/log2(i+1)); nDCG@k = DCG@k/IDCG@k. Raw DCG isn't comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents (a query with 5 relevant docs has a higher raw ceiling than one with 1), so normalizing by each query's own achievable maximum makes scores comparable across a golden set.

drills.q: What makes a golden set "not garbage," concretely?
drills.a: Real queries sampled from production plus deliberate edge cases, a 50+ query floor before trusting the metric to gate decisions, at least two independent annotators reconciling every label, graded relevance where the product needs it, and periodic refresh as the corpus changes.

drills.q: Explain the ceiling argument: why can't a reranker fix a recall miss? How would you prove that's what's happening?
drills.a: A reranker only reorders candidates first-stage retrieval already surfaced; if the answer-bearing chunk was never in the candidate set, there's nothing to promote. Prove it by measuring recall@k1 of the first stage in isolation against the golden set -- if the document isn't even in that set, the reranker is provably blameless.

drills.q: Why is a chunking miss easy to misdiagnose as a retrieval miss, and how do you tell them apart?
drills.a: Both produce the same symptom (LLM lacks the answer or hallucinates). Check whether the answer-bearing source document was retrieved at all, even split across chunks -- if the correct document is in the candidate set but no single chunk contains the full answer, that's a chunking miss, not a retrieval miss.

drills.q: Why is offline-online metric correlation often weak, and what's the practical consequence?
drills.a: Published research reports Pearson correlations around 0.3, not 0.8+. Golden sets are static curated snapshots that don't capture diversity, personalization, or real intent variance, and multi-stage interactions can offset component-level gains. Practically: treat an offline win as a hypothesis for an online A/B test, not a stopping point.

drills.q: Describe the error-analysis loop as a repeatable method rather than a one-time audit.
drills.a: Sample real failures, classify each by root cause (retrieval/ranking/chunking/generation miss) using the pipeline stages, fix whichever class is most common (not the loudest individual failure), then re-measure and repeat -- each pass should shift the dominant failure class.

drills.q: Your team has improved nDCG for two straight quarters but a user survey shows perceived answer quality hasn't moved. Diagnose.
drills.a: Two hypotheses to check: (1) nDCG may be the wrong metric if the generator ingests the whole top-k regardless of order -- Recall@k or a faithfulness metric may actually gate perceived quality. (2) Retrieval may be past its practical ceiling and the bottleneck shifted to chunking or generation -- run error analysis to see if generation misses now dominate. Either way, re-run error classification and consider switching the optimized metric rather than continuing to push the same number.

drills.q: What's ablation discipline and why does skipping it cause future regressions?
drills.a: When multiple changes ship in one bundle, an aggregate metric win doesn't reveal which component mattered -- some could be hurting while others mask it. Skipping isolation means a future engineer may remove what looks like a redundant piece of the bundle that was actually carrying the improvement, with no record of which piece that was.
